title: Samsung Galaxy Watch9 Review: Too Many Health Scores, Not Enough Battery
summary:
Samsung's new Galaxy Watch9 is a solid smartwatch, but it's a modest update from last year's Watch8. The biggest change is a faster processor, which makes scrolling and launching apps smooth. It also adds raise-to-talk for Gemini, so you can lift your wrist to your mouth and talk to Google's AI assistant. The battery is slightly bigger, but it still lasts only about 25 hours with the always-on display enabled. A full charge takes around 100 minutes—much longer than the Pixel Watch 5's 45 minutes.

The watch keeps Samsung's "squircle" shape—a circular screen inside a square bezel. The reviewer isn't a fan because it leaves unused space and collects dust in the crevices. The display is bright at 3,000 nits, so you can read it in direct sunlight. It's also water and dust resistant.

Samsung's biggest pitch is health tracking. The Watch9 adds Hearing, Vitals, Sleep Apnea, Daily Cardio Load, Fitness Index, and Heart Health Score. Some features are genuinely helpful. The Hearing feature warns you about unsafe noise levels. Vitals tracks overnight blood oxygen, heart rate, and skin temperature, and can flag when something deviates from your normal range. The FDA-cleared Sleep Apnea function can identify signs of sleep apnea.

But the reviewer is skeptical of the new fitness scores. Daily Cardio Load and Fitness Index try to boil your health down to a single number. The reviewer says these are better for spotting long-term trends than for judging your health. The Heart Health Score requires a separate blood pressure cuff to calibrate, which most people won't buy. The reviewer wishes Samsung had spent more energy refining existing features instead of piling on new scores. Still, for first-time buyers, the Watch9 is a feature-packed option.
why_it_matters: Millions of teenagers already wear a device that turns their body into a number, and this review is a reminder that a score is a rough trend, not a diagnosis. Learning to ask 'what does this number really measure, and who decided it?' is a skill that matters far beyond gadgets.

background_read: Smartwatches are one of the most crowded corners of the tech world. Samsung (the South Korean company that also makes Galaxy phones) has sold watches under the Galaxy Watch name since 2018, and Apple's Watch arrived a few years before that. Google now sells the Pixel Watch — the Pixel Watch 5 mentioned in this review — and Google's Gemini is the AI assistant built into its phones and watches.

Health tracking has become the main selling point of these devices. Watches use tiny lights on the back to shine through the skin and estimate heart rate and blood oxygen, which is why the numbers are close but not identical to hospital equipment.

Some features go much further, and that is where the FDA comes in. The FDA (the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, the government body that approves medicines and medical devices) has cleared sleep apnea detection on some Samsung watches, meaning the feature meets a safety standard similar to a medical product.

Even so, a score produced by an app is not a diagnosis. Doctors still run sleep studies or use blood pressure cuffs to check patients, and regulators generally treat 'wellness scores' as lifestyle tools rather than medical advice.

perspectives.description: For someone choosing their first smartwatch, the Watch9 packs a bright sunlight-readable screen, water resistance and genuinely useful safety tools such as noise warnings and FDA-cleared sleep apnea detection. It is a lot of features in one device.

The reviewer argues Samsung is adding scores faster than it is improving the basics. The battery still needs a slow 100-minute charge, and features like the Heart Health Score only work if you buy extra hardware, so the numbers may look impressive without changing anything.

Because phone and watch hardware improves only slightly each year, companies compete by adding software features instead. Health metrics sit in an awkward middle ground between lifestyle gadgets and medical tools, and regulators have cleared only some of them.

Battery life and charging speed are now the battleground against Google's Pixel Watch and Apple's Watch, so the next models will likely be judged on power rather than new scores. The bigger question is whether health scores eventually face the same testing and labelling rules as medical devices.
